newsitem.title: UK: British fraudbusters bouyed by BCCI conviction.
newsitem.headline: British fraudbusters bouyed by BCCI conviction.

text.p: Britain's Serious Fraud Office (SFO) on Thursday expressed satisfaction at the succesful prosecution over the BCCI bank collapse scandal in what it said was the biggest fraud trial in history.

"We are obviously very pleased (with the verdict)," SFO senior assistant director Chris Dickson told Reuters after a jury at London's Central Criminal Court found Abbas Gokal guilty of conspiring to account falsely and conspiracy to defraud.

Gokal's was the SFO's fifth consecutive conviction in its investigation and prosecution of individuals responsible for the collapse of Bank of Credit of Commerce International (BCCI) which failed in 1991, losing thousands of people their life savings.

Gokal was the former chairman of shipping and trading enterprise Gulf Group which itself collapsed in 1992 after the failure of BCCI. The SFO said he had "masterminded a massive fraud totalling approximately $1.2 billion" and now faces a maximum prison sentence of 17 years for his part in the scandal.

Dickson said he was particularly pleased with the result of the trial, which he called the biggest such case, for the "hundreds of thousands of depositors who put their life savings into BCCI and lost the lot".

He said individual cases of people who had lost money as a result of the BCCI fraud showed "the real cost" of such cases. He highlighted the example of one depositor who lost the money he had saved to pay for a bone marrow transplant for his sick son.

The SFO has come under the spotlight in recent years for failing to secure convictions in several high-profile cases but has recently had a string of successes, including the conviction earlier this week of former Resort Hotels boss Robert Feld for fraud.
Dickson said morale at the office was high.
"We feel that the SFO is in excellent shape," Dickson said. "George Staple has done an excellent job and is handing over to his successor Rosalind Wright a ship that is in excellent shape," he added.

Staple, who has been director of the SFO for the past five years, is due to return to private practice with law firm Clifford Chance later this month. His successor Wright will become the fourth SFO director.

When she takes over the reins she will become the second woman to run the office, which investigates and prosecutes Britain's most serious and complex financial fraud cases. She joins from financial markets watchdog the Securities and Futures Authority.
The SFO was set up in 1988 with the aim of bringing more of these complicated white-collar crimes to trial and putting the perpetrators behind bars.
It has fought an uphill battle against unfavourable public and media opinion following several high-profile acquittals and perceived "failures" to get convictions.
These have included the acquittal of former boxer George Walker in 1994 for an alleged 164 million pound ($269.1 million) fraud on creditors and shareholders in his leisure group Brent Walker.

The acquittal of Kevin and Ian Maxwell almost a year ago on fraud charges and the subsequent throwing out of a second trial against Kevin, son of the late tycoon Robert Maxwell, were also viewed as blows.
But public perception of its performance is at odds with its ability to prosecute cases and get convictions. The SFO's overall conviction rate since its inception is running at around 63 percent.

One legal source said the Gokal conviction also strengthened flagging confidence in the use of the jury trial system in complex frauds. The Gokal trial began last September and lasted nearly five months.

"This is a good result for those who say juries can cope with long trials," he said. There have been calls for scrapping jury trials by those who argue lay jurors cannot get to grips with such complex cases.
Some have suggested a panel of experts should be used to try such cases but this is seen as being at odds with Britain's judicial tradition. ($ = 0.609 British Pounds)
